When: 7:00 pm CST. Where: Fiserv Forum—Milwaukee, WI. Watch: MY24. Listen: Check local listings . Prescient Prediction The Celtics lead by at least 15 points by the end of the first quarter. The Celtics led Milwaukee 28-14 by the end of the first frame in their last meeting, and that was without Tatum. Boston’s aggressive defense could give the streaky Bucks a tough time, and the C’s have the star power on offense to make this a one-sided affair.

stories.title: Sixers visit Bulls for second meeting in Sunday matinee
stories.summary: After suffering their second defeat of the season on Friday night, the Sixers have an opportunity to write the ship against a struggling Bulls squad.
stories.detailText: The Philadelphia 76ers have one more game on this road trip before they head home, visiting the Chicago Bulls on Sunday afternoon. This is the second time in under a week the Sixers and Bulls are meeting, with the Sixers winning their first foray 126-107 back on Monday. With the Bulls going into that contest 1-5, some may have expected the then 6-1 Sixers to have handled that game with ease… but it took until the final few minutes for Philadelphia to finally pull away from Chicago. Since then, the Bulls have dropped to 1-7 on the season, and come into Sunday on a six-game skid. Looking at the injury reports, Joel Embiid is currently probable for Sunday's contest due to plantar fasciitis management. Not sure if it was what was bothering him on Friday, but he certainly seemed off in that one to say the least. And the hits just keep coming at the center position for Philadelphia with Adem Bona ruled out for a second consecutive game due to a cervical spine sprain. This may mean that — for better or worse —there's more pressure on Embiid to play even if he isn't 100% right now. The only other injury note for the Sixers are that Dominick Barlow (back) remains out. For the Bulls, there is some mystery around who may be playing center for them tomorrow as well. Nic Claxton is currently listed as questionable after being sidelined to start the season with a hamstring strain. Him being listed as questionable is a step toward the direction of the Bulls' starting center possibly taking the floor against the Sixers. Jalen Smith, who has been starting at the five in Claxton's absence, is probable with a left finger sprain. Also for Chicago, Tobe Awaka is questionable while Zach Collins and Dailyn Swain are out. The Bulls will have the rest advantage this afternoon as they haven't played since Wednesday for some unknown reason. Who am I to question the wisdom of the NBA schedule makers? Earlier this week, the Sixers utilized a widespread effort across their starters to get the job done against the Bulls. All five starters scored in the double-digits, and three scored more than 20 points each. It was an especially impressive night from VJ Edgecombe, who shot 9-for-12 from the floor and 2-for-4 from behind the arc for 21 points. Tyrese Maxey had a 26-point, 11 assist double-double, Jaylen Brown added a 25-point, 11-rebound double-double, and LeBron James posted 15 points and nine assists — some of which were just incredible displays of playmaking. I'm a big believer in "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". One of the things the Sixers did exceptionally well in that contest was getting out in transition on a clinical level. A shot would go up on the defensive end, James would be ready to rebound as Edgecombe or Maxey preemptively charged up the floor. A few incredible, quarterback-level passes from James and the Sixers enjoyed the benefits of taking the easy buckets as they came. That last part is my advice for the Sixers tonight: don't make it harder than it needs to be. Take the easy buckets out in stride when you can get them. Don't let the Bulls grab offensive rebound after offensive rebound for second chance points. Don't rely on one player to do all the heavy lifting. Spread the floor and the ball, and don't turn it into a battle to the end with a team that is objectively worse. If you can, get a lead big enough that even Nick Nurse gives the starting five a little rest toward the end. Coming off just their second loss of the season, one can imagine the Sixers coming into Sunday with a strong desire to right the ship. Right there with them is a Bulls squad that is desperately trying to find their footing this season and may have their starting center back in the mix. Regardless, this is one that the Sixers really should win, barring any major changes to the injury reports pregame. But we all know how well "should" goes in the NBA. The Sixers and Bulls tip off at 3:30 p.m. ET. Game Details When: Sunday, November 8, 3:30 p.m. ET Where: United Center, Chicago, IL Watch: NBC Sports Philadelphia Radio: 97.5 The Fanatic Follow: @LibertyBallers

stories.title: Rockets hit first losing streak of season, fall 102-99 to Suns
stories.summary: Houston has their first losing streak of the season.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, ARIZONA - NOVEMBER 07: Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns drives to the basket against Kevin Durant #7 of the Houston Rockets during the second half of the game at Mortgage Matchup Center on November 07, 2026 in Phoenix, Arizona. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Rockets hit their first losing streak of the season on Saturday night, as they let the Suns run all over them to start, battled back, but then couldn’t close out the game. For their last loss against Minnesota, it was a ghost of last season — execution — that was a main culprit. This time, it was shooting. The Rockets couldn’t hit the broad side of the barn, and you have to credit the Phoenix defense. They looked like the fresher team in the fourth quarter, when they shot 11-for-22 from the field, while the Rockets were only 10-for-27. In fact, for the game, Houston shot just 38 percent from the field, while allowing the Suns to shoot 48 percent. You’re not gonna win many that way. In fact, the only Rocket player with a semi-decent game was Jabari Smith Jr., who continues to break out this season offensively. Smith went for 15 points on 7-for-12 shooting, 9 rebounds, 2 assists, 3 steals and a block, though he was just 1-for-4 from deep. Still, Smith was the only Rockets player who could hit some shots outside of Fred VanVleet. FVV went for 16 points, 3 rebounds, and 4 assists while shooting 6-for-12 from the floor and 4-for-9 from deep. VanVleet mostly played a clean game with zero turnovers, however, you want to see greater assist numbers, and with the offense stuck in the mud most of the game, you also want to see a greater impact from a distribution standpoint. But when no one is hitting shots… Kevin Durant led the Rockets in scoring with 21 points, and he also had 10 boards and 3 assists, but he shot just 5-for-14 for the game, including 1-for-5 in a decisive fourth quarter that the Rockets lost. Alperen Sengun had 15 points, but he was just 5-for-16 from the field. Houston’s bench also shot just 6-for-25 for the game, including a combined 3-for-16 from Tari Eason and Reed Sheppard. Reed played just 13 minutes in this one, and it is increasingly appearing he is the odd man out in the rotation, especially if the three isn’t falling — and it wasn’t on Saturday at just 2-for-6 from deep. The Suns were led by Devin Booker’s 24 points, while former Rocket Jalen Green had 16 points and 6 assists, and other former Rocket Dillon Brooks had 11 points and 4 boards while hitting 3 triples. Houston falls to 7-3 on the season, and after a fast start (just like last year), some warts are starting to appear (just like last year), including late-game execution, overall shooting, and rotation management, again many of the same issues as last season. Nevertheless, the team is currently on a 57-win pace, but with the Western Conference wide open this year, you’d like to see the Rockets looking a little tighter. The team returns to action Monday night at home against the Denver Nuggets.

stories.title: Bucks Reacts Survey Results: The Bucks are too nice, fans aren’t, and both of these are okay!
stories.summary: No need to check your list twice for these guys, Santa.

(Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, despite the losses, Bucks fans were happy—if not more—with Taylor Jenkins and his rotations. But something about that equation was worrisome. In fact, I pondered as much to end the week’s Bucks Reacts Results : With rotation contentment high but wins low, the question thus begs: how long can this relationship coexist? That is, how long will it be until the losing takes its toll? Here’s hoping that becomes a moot point. This week, as the losses start to mount and the shine of a new season appears to be rubbing off, that point has not become moot. And, as the saying goes, nice guys finish last. Chivalry isn’t dead (but maybe it should be) Yes, according to most fans—66% in fact—you’ll find these Milwaukee Bucks helping out at The Leftorium, reading to underprivileged kids, or helping your grandmother cross the street. They’re too nice. And their new mantra’s got nothin’ on ye olde one: Naughty or nice, these Bucks suck But it’s not really a question of demeanour, at least according to a swathe of commenters. From their perspective, the Bucks are simply not talented enough: Yikes. Talk about glass all empty. Contrary to the point Perhaps, though, it’s not about whether the Bucks are too nice or not talented enough. Perhaps it’s an “intensity and urgency” matter. Sounds awfully familiar to “energy and effort.” That you, Jason? Finally, at least one fan hasn’t forgotten that time is a key part of the re build: Thankfully, with Nate Ament (19), Kasparas Jakučionis (20), Brayden Burries (21), Kel’el Ware (22), Ousmane Dieng (23), and Ryan Rollins (24), these Bucks have plenty of time. And at least a few of ‘em are already ahead of the curve. There you have it, BH fam. While these Bucks may be too nice, that’s not a bad position to start from. After all, as Laurell K. Hamilton wrote in her 2005 novel A Stroke of Midnight : My father had taught me to be nice first, because you can always be mean later, but once you’ve been mean to someone, they won’t believe the nice anymore. So be nice, be nice, until it’s time to stop being nice, then destroy them. That’s right, the Bucks might be in the trenches, but a fire brews.

stories.title: Making sense of Jaylen Brown's previous impact with Celtics
stories.summary: Ahead of the 76ers-Celtics game, we dive into the gap between Brown and on/off statistics.
stories.detailText: If the Dallas Mavericks ' infamous trade of Luka Doncic produced waves of shock and outrage across the NBA, then the Boston Celtics ' trade of Jaylen Brown a year later was met with considerably more complicated reactions. Outrage, yes, from Celtics fans -- but also a fierce debate about Brown's on-court value and broader questions about how to analyze players in the modern, data-infused NBA. Brown is a five-time All-Star, a former Finals MVP and the sixth-place finisher in regular-season MVP voting in 2026, after he averaged a career-best 28.7 points per game. Yet, advanced stats were more skeptical of his stardom. The Celtics had a better net rating with Brown off the court than on it in seven of his 10 seasons in Boston, including each of the last four. (All on/off data in this piece comes from Cleaning the Glass, which strips out garbage time.) With Brown poised to play against his old team for the first time on Tuesday ( 8 p.m. ET, NBC/Peacock ) -- and with the NBA's best current rivalry poised to begin a new chapter -- it's the perfect time for a deeper dive into what exactly the gap between Brown's reputation and advanced stats means, and how it contributed to the summer's blockbuster trade. Given the statistics explosion in the NBA's ongoing information era, it's easy to access on/off numbers for every player in the league. Based on conversations with both public and team-side analysts, here's the best way to understand how to interpret them. Jump to topic: The on/off basics Interpreting the use of on/off How on/off contributed to Brown's trade The on/off basics A modern NBA front office is inundated with data about every player in the league. Points, rebounds, assists, shot quality, pick-and-roll frequency, isolation efficiency, jump shot release point, maximum footspeed, average body orientation on closeouts, and on and on and on. The list of individual data points is nearly endless, but in theory, they all serve the same goal: A front office should identify players who can help the team outscore its opponents, rather than players who collect strong statistics in a vacuum. Often, the players with the best individual stats also provide the most winning impact -- but not always. And those occasional mismatches can yield different and sometimes counterintuitive evaluations of players. Consider the highly drafted duo in Orlando's frontcourt. Former No. 1 pick Paolo Banchero has more career points, rebounds and assists per game than teammate Franz Wagner . But Banchero has a negative or neutral on/off split in every season of his career -- meaning the Magic have always been better with him off the floor -- whereas Wagner has finished with a strongly positive on/off split every season. Most of that gap comes on defense: The Magic's defensive rating has been 3.8 points higher with Banchero on the floor across his tenure, while it has been 5.4 points lower with Wagner on the court. Wagner doesn't generate many steals or blocks, but the idea behind on/off data is that he's clearly doing something right on that end, even if it doesn't show up in the box score. Ask folks around the league about the profile of a player who's more valuable than his basic stats suggest, and they'll often talk about defensive standouts. That group includes players such as Alex Caruso and OG Anunoby , who have played major roles for the past two champions. They've followed in the footsteps of Shane Battier, famously dubbed the " No-Stats All-Star " in a 2009 piece by author Michael Lewis. It's no surprise that those role players posted exemplary on/off numbers throughout their careers. But that reputation can take a very long time to stabilize. An analyst for an Eastern Conference team said that 10,000 possessions, or about two seasons of data for a starter, is the minimum sample size before on/off data starts becoming useful. That caution runs counter to the incessant need for information and analysis, even when the new season's samples are unsuitably tiny in early November. For instance, it's tempting to look at Amen Thompson 's early on/off data point for the 2026-27 season and think there's something wrong with his development: The Rockets have been a whopping 47.3 points per 100 possessions worse with him on the floor through nine games, by far the worst mark for any rotation player in the NBA. But experts know that's the wrong way to interpret the data, and they haven't come close to downgrading their opinion of Thompson's value yet. "The public should not have access to on/off this early in the season," the East analyst said. "It should be banned. I think it's a disservice to the discourse." Transforming on/off data from 'astrology' to analysis The problem with on/off data in its raw, preliminary form is that it's subject to all sorts of inherent biases, including that sample size issue. "I call it astrology for NBA professionals," said an executive for a Western Conference team, "because whatever story you want to tell, you can go and [find confirmation]." For this reason, professional analysts say they don't typically work with on/off data until they've made a host of adjustments. To transform on/off data from astrology to analysis, they employ an advanced statistical technique called regularized adjusted plus-minus, or RAPM, which adds in various adjustments to refine the raw data. This process "does a much better job of understanding context and isolating the player's actual impact," said Taylor Snarr, a former analyst for the Jazz and creator of the advanced stat estimated plus-minus (EPM). Depending on the specific model, RAPM controls for factors such as: The identity of the other nine players on the court (four teammates and five opponents) Home-court advantage When teams are in the bonus The opponent's 3-point and free throw percentages, which aren't affected by individual defenders The "rubber band effect," which shows that teams play worse when they're ahead by a large margin (like a rubber band snapping back) Whether a defense is playing in front of its own bench, which can improve performance The most important is the first bullet point, largely because it can account for situations in which the same players "are playing together frequently and consistently," Snarr said. Two years ago, for instance, Christian Braun finished with the third-best on/off swing among rotation players -- but Nikola Jokic finished first, and Braun shared the court with Jokic for the vast majority of his minutes. Without properly adjusting for his teammates, it would look as if Braun -- who is still a solid contributor but not in the elite echelon -- was one of the NBA's most valuable players. For advanced player value models such as EPM, the next step is to incorporate what's called a "box score prior," which means blending box score statistics into the adjusted on/off mix to give credit to the right players. (Some models also incorporate various amounts of advanced tracking data at this point.) In that Nuggets example, Jokic's box score stats are far superior to Braun's, so the model can be more confident that Jokic is the main driver of that extraordinary on/off split. These adjustments allow for much quicker, more accurate analysis of players because of how they isolate impact. "Instead of taking 10 years for on/off to be convincing, you can reduce it down to maybe two years with RAPM," said Kostya Medvedovsky, creator of the DARKO projection system. This general process is now fairly routine for NBA model builders. But it can be more of an art than a science, and the trickier question is "how heavily do you prefer the [box score] statistical components versus the on/off components," the Western executive said. "That's where I think there becomes more of a legitimate debate and variance amongst the nerds." For a player like Jaylen Brown, whose traditional stats far outshine his on/off impact, that debate plays an outsized impact in his evaluation. If a player value model weights box score stats heavily, then it will likely conclude that Brown is an elite player because of his strong scoring and all-around production. But if a model weights box score stats less and on/off data more, then it won't be as impressed with the former Finals MVP. Brown's on/off impact on Boston's offense was typically mediocre because he had poor efficiency for a high-usage player and he posted too many turnovers to too few assists. Public RAPM-style metrics generally consider Brown to be a very good player but not an MVP-caliber alpha. That mismatch is just one reason that his trade was so controversial. How on/off might have contributed to the Brown trade It's hard to deny that the proliferation of on/off-based metrics in both the public discourse and NBA front offices has transformed the league over the past couple of decades. "I think what's changed the most is the acceptance among nontechnical people," the Western Conference executive said. "Not because they've sat down and taken in those lessons [from analytics], but just because the way everyone understands players has shifted, I think because of the success of those kinds of metrics in helping teams identify and evaluate talent." It helps that many of the best-run franchises clearly abide by the principles of adjusted on/off data. Executives point to the Celtics and Thunder as two of the teams best known for "RAPM maxxing," which is observable from the kinds of players those teams tend to acquire. Derrick White , Isaiah Hartenstein and Caruso have always rated well by adjusted on/off metrics. In fact, Caruso's teams have been better with him on the court in all nine of his NBA campaigns, across three separate organizations and two championships. There's a reason both DARKO and EPM rate Caruso as a top-30 player in the league on a per-possession basis, even though he has never averaged more than 10.1 points per game in a season. Granted, not every RAPM-influenced move is going to be a slam dunk. Analysts point to the Thunder's acquisitions of Patrick Patterson in 2017 and Gordon Hayward in 2024 , who were both RAPM darlings before busting in Oklahoma City. Patterson notably posted double-digit on/off swings in the positive direction in his last two seasons in Toronto, right before posting double-digit on/off swings in the negative direction in his two seasons in Oklahoma City. But those unsuccessful acquisitions didn't stop the Thunder from continuing to trust their models, rival analysts say. And it's that mindset that led them to add Hartenstein and Caruso in the same summer. The Thunder were champions a year later, with Caruso maintaining his positive on/off streak in each season with Oklahoma City so far. Another player with positive on/off splits in every season of his career is Paul George , across his stints in Indiana, Oklahoma City, LA and Philadelphia. Just one glance at this graph comparing the yearly on/off splits for George and Brown shows why Boston might have preferred to trade the latter for the former, even before considering financial considerations, draft picks or Brown's behind-the-scenes fit in Boston. Many league insiders were still taken aback by the Celtics' return for an MVP candidate in his prime when they dealt Brown to Philadelphia for George -- who, despite his impressive on/off track record, is older, injury-prone and highly paid -- and picks over the summer. But it wasn't exactly a secret that Boston wanted to trade Brown, so other interested teams had the opportunity to beat the 76ers' offer if they thought signing the Finals MVP was worth a higher cost. That no better offer came demonstrates just how deeply the lessons of adjusted on/off metrics have permeated the thinking of most front offices. "In some ways, the Jaylen Brown case is the purest proof of this," Medvedovsky said. "It seemed like: You're trading a Finals MVP, so you're going to get a ton of value for him. But then we saw you just didn't." This wasn't a case of one ahead-of-his-time, outside-the-box general manager making a shrewd move; rather, it was a case of 28 other general managers not making an all-in offer for a player with underwhelming adjusted on/off metrics. Now in Philadelphia, however, Brown is attempting to prove that there should have been a massive market for his services: He's averaging 21.6 points per game while often serving as the third or fourth option on the East-leading, 8-2 76ers. And while it's far too soon to come to any meaningful conclusions about Philadelphia's performance splits with and without him -- Brown has played just 678 possessions as a Sixer, per Cleaning the Glass, or less than 10% of the way to 10,000 -- one early-season data point is mighty compelling. With Brown on the floor, the 76ers have outscored their opponents by 4.3 points per 100 possessions; without him, they're at minus-1.9. That 6.2-point swing, if sustained, would represent the second-best single-season on/off of Brown's career. "With [Daryl] Morey gone," Medvedovsky added, "there's no GM who I would identify as, this is the stats GM . But in some ways, it's like a total victory for the on/off data that even with no visibly stats GM, even the non-stats people were on/off-pilled enough that there just wasn't that kind of massive market for Jaylen Brown."

stories.title: Against Oklahoma City, the Wizards were the bug
stories.summary: Oklahoma City Thunder broadcaster Michael Cage summed up this game perfectly: “In this game, sometimes you’re the bug, and sometimes you’re the windshield.” In this one, the Wizards were in the role of the bug. Washington was no match for the Thunder. Oklahoma City took control early and the Wizards had no answer for …
stories.detailText: Oklahoma City Thunder broadcaster Michael Cage summed up this game perfectly: “In this game, sometimes you’re the bug, and sometimes you’re the windshield.” In this one, the Wizards were in the role of the bug. Washington was no match for the Thunder. Oklahoma City took control early and the Wizards had no answer for their athleticism, execution, and swarming defensive presence. The Wizards converted just 29.6% of their field goal attempts, including 7-43 from three-point range. That’s 16.3%. Which is bad. Very bad. Positives for the Wizards were scarce. Among them — Alex Sarr grabbed 14 rebounds in 28 minutes. Bub Carrington shot 3-3 from deep. Bilal Coulibaly defended Shai Gilgeous-Alexander pretty well in the first quarter — SGA had two points on o-3 shooting when Coulibaly left the game. He immediately started scoring and finished the game with 30 points and 9 assists. For Washington, it’s a third consecutive loss — their first three-game skid of the season. Before the game, head coach Brian Keefe talked with reporters about the team figuring out their formula for success. The team would be wise not to over-index on this game. It was a bad result, and the team looked awful. Despite missing Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren (in some order, their second and third best players), OKC is a special case. It’s a championship-level team with something to prove. The Wizards need to learn to compete at that level, and the lesson of their last three games is that they’re still not close. That’s not the end of world 10 games into the season. But they need to internalize that lesson and do the work to become competitive against high-level opponents. From the Notebook Kudos to the OKC stadium operations team — when the Wizards starters got introduced, they played Harry Potter theme music. Good job. The Wizards entered the game with the NBA’s second best “in the paint” field goal percentage (62.2%). The Thunder had the NBA’s second best defensive paint FG% (holding opponents to just 50.2%). Safe to say OKC won that battle. In the first quarter, the Wizards ran a pick-and-roll option out of a horns set for AJ Dybantsa. He had a choice of going left or right. It didn’t go great — he ended up battling his way into a mid-ranger, which he missed. The set was good, though. Tre Mann got real minutes for the first time this season. He looked pretty good — quick, aggressive, athletic. I’d like to see more. Jotted during the second quarter (could have been jotted anytime) — OKC defenders switch HARD. Another second quarter note — OKC was doubling Trae Young to get the ball out of his hands. The other Wizards weren’t able to take make plays, in part because OKC defenders hustled back to their matchups and rotated so perfectly. I thought maybe the Wizards had a chance of making things respectable — a thought that disappeared when I saw their possession of the second half. It was a pick-and-roll for Kyshawn George, who got caught in no-man’s land. The only teammate who cut was Coulibaly, who didn’t get free. That should have triggered a cascade of movement, but the other guys stood around until George was forced to take a difficult shot, which he missed. The Wizards tried a small-ball lineup in the second half. It got shredded by Aday Mara and the Thunder.

stories.title: Phoenix bent but never broke against the Rockets
stories.summary: Phoenix displayed the mental toughness and defensive identity that defined its success a season ago.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, AZ - NOVEMBER 7: Luke Kennard #8 of the Phoenix Suns handles the ball during the game against the Houston Rockets on November 7, 2026 at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix, Arizona. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Barry Gossage/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Saturday night’s victory over the Houston Rockets was easily the Phoenix Suns’ best win of the season. Granted, they’ve only won three games through their first eight, but this one felt different. Phoenix continued its recent trend of putting together quality first quarters, something that has become increasingly important given how frequently this team has found itself playing from behind. When the Suns fall into an early deficit, players tend to press, forcing the issue offensively and abandoning the systems and schemes designed to put them in positions to succeed. But Saturday night presented a different kind of adversity. After building a lead that reached as many as 19 points, the Suns completely unraveled in the second quarter. They managed a miserable 12 points, shot 3-of-11 from beyond the arc, and apparently decided to let amber be the color of their energy as Houston closed the half on a 22-3 run to erase the deficit entirely (that’s a 311 joke). What had been a commanding Phoenix advantage was suddenly a tie game heading into the locker room. And that’s where things got interesting. Throughout the second half, we witnessed a collection of quality performances from different players on both ends of the floor. There were timely offensive contributions, defensive adjustments, and moments when individual effort helped stabilize a team that had every reason to start questioning itself. By the time the final buzzer sounded, the Suns had earned a 102-99 victory over one of the NBA’s most potent offenses. That’s right. For the first time this season, Phoenix held an opponent under 100 points. And that opponent happened to be the Houston Rockets. That accomplishment alone makes this victory impressive, but what stands out even more is how the Suns responded after their complete second-quarter meltdown. When you surrender a 19-point advantage in such a short period of time, it’s easy to fold. It’s easy to begin doubting yourself, questioning whether you have the personnel, discipline, or defensive capability to stop the opponent standing across from you. We’ve seen that uncertainty creep into this team’s play far too often through the opening weeks of the season. Saturday night, however, was the first time we truly witnessed the mental toughness and fortitude that defined this team a season ago. The Suns refused to let one disastrous quarter dictate the outcome of the game. They regrouped, stood tall, and collectively found a way to shut down a Houston offense that had been operating like a well-oiled machine. In doing so, they earned, in every sense of the word, their third victory of the season. stories.title: Diving deeper into Cavs 109-97 loss to Knicks: The more things change, the more they stay the same
stories.summary: It’s the same story, just a different day.
stories.detailText: Nov 7, 2026; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) throws a pass in front of Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell (45) in the first quarter at Rocket Arena. Mandatory Credit: David Richard-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect CLEVELAND — The Cleveland Cavaliers couldn’t keep up with a New York Knicks team that just has their number. They dropped Saturday’s game 109-97 . Three stars of the game First star: Jalen Brunson 31 points, 9 assists, 6 rebounds Brunson is a certified Cavs killer. He picked up right where he left off last postseason by torching whatever defender Cleveland put in front of him. He got inside the paint and to his midrange floater with ease. And when he didn’t, the outside shot was working as well. There really isn’t much that you can do when Brunson has it going as he did here. The Cavs sent some doubles at him and tried to shade their defense toward him. When they got too far, he made the easy pass to the open teammate, never forcing anything. The Cavs’ strategy was fine. The defense also wasn’t necessarily horrible. Cleveland’s guards competed, but that didn’t matter. Brunson is just too good a shot and decision-maker. Second star: Donovan Mitchell 37 points, 4 assists, 4 rebounds, 2 steals, 1 block Mitchell is putting together an impressive season from a process standpoint. He’s doing a better job of looking for his teammates, while also finding avenues to score. “I think the biggest thing is creating an opportunity,” Mitchell said. “I haven’t shot as many shots as I have in my career, so trying to balance that and figure out trying to make the right basketball play. Sometimes that is shooting. Sometimes that is passing. Sometimes that is running the blitz, and it’s going to help to make me better.” Mitchell tried to will the Cavs back into this game, scoring 21 in the final quarter alone. But as impressive as he was, a one-man army wasn’t enough to take down a well-oiled machine like the Knicks. Especially when the rest of his co-stars struggled. Third star: Karl-Anthony Towns 29 points, 13 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 steals Towns is such a difficult player to defend. His outside shot requires him to be guarded out on the perimeter, which opens up the lane for his teammates. If the defensive center leaves, Towns can make them pay with the outside shot. And, if his defender closes out too hard, Towns is quick enough off the dribble to make them pay inside. This was on display on Saturday. He drew two quick fouls on Mobley in the first quarter by attacking the rim. This changed the complexion of the game. Without Jarrett Allen, the Cavs were forced to turn to third-string center Thomas Bryant for a longer stretch than they would’ve ideally liked. Towns’s presence can completely change an offense as dynamic as New York’s. Cleveland found that out again the hard way. Duds of the game James Harden 7 points on 2-of-9 shooting, 5 assists, 2 rebounds, 2 blocks The Cavs offense can look lifeless when Harden isn’t able to get downhill. On Saturday, he was a step slow and couldn’t create any separation off the dribble. That limited his effectiveness. On the other end, the Knicks continually hunted him in mismatches. To his credit, Harden competed. But it wasn’t enough to keep this from being a winning strategy. This has been less than an ideal start to the season for Harden. Evan Mobley 12 points, 9 rebounds, 5 assists, 3 turnovers Mobley’s ability to win the matchup over Joel Embiid was a deciding factor in Cleveland’s runaway win over the Philadelphia 76ers . Likewise, his inability to do so against New York contributed to the loss. The foul trouble made it difficult for Mobley to establish any kind of offense inside. This left him as mostly a jump shooter at the start of the game. And since the three-ball wasn’t falling (1-for-5 on the evening), there wasn’t much he was capable of offensively to help jumpstart an offense that needed it. Cavalier who deserves a shoutout Peyton Watson 12 points, 6 rebounds, 3 assists Watson was useful in this game. He provided some much-needed offense and was helpful as a defender. That’s what you want to see from Watson in this matchup. Play of the game watch Don on the ground 😂 Made sure to find Knecht and shoot him with the spida webs pic.twitter.com/nkby46hYtE — Mikey McNuggets (@MikeLucasTV) November 8, 2026 Quote of the day “Not really. In Jauary we went 2-9. I’m not really into measuring stick games). … Let’s say we win by 15. Well, we might get hammered next week by whoever’s in last place by 20. Does that mean we suck? No. You just take it one game at a time and try to get a little bit better.” – Knicks head coach Mike Brown before the game when asked if this was a measuring stick game It’s tempting to use this difficult stretch of games as a test for where the Cavs are. And if you were going to use it as one, they wouldn’t necessarily pass. The more concerning thing is the lack of discernible identity. When they’re playing well, the Cavs can beat anyone, as we saw against Philadelphia. But what does this group hang their hat on? What does better look like for them? And are they taking steps to get there? Those are the questions that matter, and we don’t have clear answers for any of them. Stat of the game The Knicks outscored the Cavs 26-8 in second-chance points. New York retrieved 41.8% of their missed shots ( 94th percentile ). And then they made the most of those opportunities by scoring a quarter’s worth of points on that alone. “We have to rebound better collectively,” head coach Kenny Atkinson said. “There’s no one pointing the finger. The guys got to do it collectively. We just got to be better.” Main takeaway from this game: The Knicks have the Cavs number I don’t necessarily think the Knicks present stylistic problems that the Cavs can’t solve. An offense that hunts out mismatches with their smaller, but electric, scoring guard isn’t something the Cavs should, on paper, be incapable of countering. Yet, the Cavs are consistently ending up on the wrong side of this matchup. The Knicks have their number, and there’s no way around that. Atkinson and Mitchell were asked what makes this matchup so difficult afterward. Both pointed to the offensive rebounding as an obvious issue, and one that we all can see. They also both mentioned that the Knicks just understand how to play with each other and use that to seize the openings teams give them. “They really have solutions,” Atkinson said. “I think their continuity…they just have great chemistry. They’re on a string on both ends.” “They’ve been through stuff together as a group,” Mitchell said. “They do a good job os seizing mistakes.” Brunson and Towns were tremendous once again tonight. Their shotmaking carried them in this matchup. But they also did a great job of accepting what the Cavs threw at them, and then having a plan of action for that. If you doubled Brunson, he moved the ball to the open teammate and made the Cavs’ defense scramble out. Conversely, when they threw doubles at Mitchell, the Cavs weren’t quick to respond. Watson admitted afterward that he doesn’t know to help Mitchell in that situation and that there are “some questions” about their strategy that he would like to ask about. That isn’t the sign of a team that’s on a string and understands what they need to do to be the best version of themselves. Little things like that are why the Knicks have been better. They understand what they need to do, and the pieces fit together perfectly to make that happen. The Cavs don’t have that right now. And until they do, they won’t be able to get through the roadblock the Knicks have become throughout this era of Cavs basketball.

stories.title: Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup
stories.summary: The Sixers fell to their second loss of the season on Friday night in Cleveland.
stories.detailText: Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers couldn’t rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers. They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4. The Sixers’ top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17). The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley. The Sixers’ injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury. With Friday’s loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat. The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland: Nightmare start for Embiid, Sixers After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam. The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers’ Oct. 22 win over Cleveland , they were many levels below their best in the first quarter. The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers’ chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter. Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid’s larger problem was that he couldn’t hit any sort of shot besides free throws. He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds. Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he’s now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that’s bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season. Of course, it’s notable that Embiid’s been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We’ll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out. James didn’t play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers. As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc. Edgecombe shrugs off foul trouble Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers’ rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures. With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland’s lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass. Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals. Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers’ comeback push. Cavs polish it off in 2nd half The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk. With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons , Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game. Still, the Sixers’ offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points. Embiid didn’t play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He’s had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career , back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors. Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they’d hit speed bumps throughout the year. They’ll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

stories.detailText: Bona doubtful, no Sixers starters on injury report for Cavs game originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia The Sixers listed backup center Adem Bona as doubtful for their Friday night meeting with the Cavaliers. Bona’s official listing on the team’s Thursday evening injury report was “cervical spine sprain.” He played one of his better games so far this season Wednesday in the 8-1 Sixers’ win over the Pistons , slamming in two second-quarter dunks and posting five points, two rebounds, a steal and an assist in 15 minutes. Bona headed back to the Sixers’ locker room with 8:56 left in the fourth quarter. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters postgame that the 23-year-old big man had “neck soreness” after taking a hit. Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear) will remain out for the Sixers in Cleveland. The Sixers beat the 4-4 Cavs in dramatic fashion on Oct. 22, overcoming a 29-point deficit to win a wild home opener. If Bona were to miss Friday’s game, Jabari Walker would be the logical next name in line at center behind Joel Embiid. Notably, the Sixers included no starters on their injury report. teamStories.detailText: PORTLAND, OREGON - NOVEMBER 07: Victor Wembanyama #1 of the San Antonio Spurs dunks the ball past Toumani Camara #33 of the Portland Trail Blazers during the second half at Moda Center on November 07, 2026 in Portland, Oregon. (Photo by Soobum Im/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you’ve been looking for a signature San Antonio Spurs win early in the 2026-27 season, look no further. On the second game of a back-to-back, the Spurs waltzed into enemy territory and blew out a team motivated to get revenge. It was one of the first times we’ve seen this year’s Spurs put it all together against a playoff-caliber team. Defense was the name of the game in San Antonio’s 125-103 win over the Portland Trail Blazers. Both teams played incredibly physical (or just flopped a lot). But the Spurs were the enforcers overall. Stephon Castle set the tone on the perimeter with some suffocating defense on two of the Blazers’ best players, Deni Advija and Jrue Holiday. Advija was particularly frustrated by Castle’s defense, scoring just 15 points on 5-13 shooting. The rest of the team forced turnovers. Portland coughed it up 18 times, leading to 23 easy points for the Spurs. The tape will show that the Spurs dominated this game with force and athleticism. The stat sheet shows they won a lot of the hustle stats, too. San Antonio won the rebounding battle by 13 and grabbed 14 offensive boards. The force they showed against Portland is the same as what they showed last season in their NBA Finals run, but more refined. The Blazers just feel like a team the Spurs will have to beat in the Victor Wembanyama era. They are young (for the most part), tough, and skilled. Beating them down in such a dominant fashion after the playoff victory last season is a clear sign that San Antonio has not taken a step back, despite some bumps to start the season. It also showed a lot of grit and edge from the Spurs. It was exactly the type of victory this team needed early in the season. Takeaways: I gave the second unit a tough time in the last WWL. They were MUCH better against Portland. Luke Kornet in particular had one of his best games of the season with 6 points, 4 rebounds, 2 assists, and a block. There were fewer moments when Kornet needed to go one-on-one with a driver at the rim, as the perimeter defense made it harder for the Blazers to get clear drives to the basket. What was even more impressive about Kornet’s game is that he actually took a few shots when he was open. Typically, the backup center isn’t even thinking about shooting, but he hit a pop-a-shot early in the game and took a jumper from the free-throw line that didn’t fall. Just getting Kornet to take those kinds of shots when they are available will help the second-unit offense tremendously. It’s been a minute since we got a sub-25-minute elite performance from Wembanyama. Not because the performances haven’t been elite, but because he’s usually playing more than 25 minutes. He had 29 points on 9-for-13 shooting, including three triples. Portland had absolutely no answer for the early-season MVP candidate. In the last two games, he’s become more selective with his jump shots, and the results have been better looks that are going in more often. Carter Bryant got an opportunity to play early in the game and made the most of it. He hit a pair of three-pointers, got a deflection and a block, providing energy off the bench. Bryant still struggles with overaggressiveness on defense. He picked up 5 fouls in just 17 minutes on Saturday. Bryant has a lot of talent; it just needs to be harnessed with improved awareness and experience. The Blazers continued their strategy of guarding Castle with Donovan Clingan and putting Toumani Camara on Wembanyama. It’s safe to say the Spurs have figured out how to defeat that coverage. It helps that Castle made two of his five three-pointers, and Wembanyama is a game-breaker. Portland still needed to send doubles at Wembanyama, and when they did, the Spurs were able to get easy looks when the ball was passed out.

teamStories.detailText: PORTLAND, OREGON - NOVEMBER 07: Deni Avdija #8 of the Portland Trail Blazers attempts a layup against Luke Kornet #7 of the San Antonio Spurs during the first half at Moda Center on November 07, 2026 in Portland, Oregon. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Soobum Im/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last season, the Spurs had the second-best record in the league on the second night of back-to-backs, and surely their youth played a role in that. Believe it or not, they’re still young just a few months later, and they are now 3-0 on SEGABABA’s this season after an absolute beatdown of the Portland Trail Blazers for their 8th straight win. Portland started the season hot but were coming off a loss to the Lakers last night, and while they may have been revenge-minded for their first-round loss in the playoffs, they were missing Ja Morant, Robert Williams and Shaedon Sharpe and were no match for a healthy Spurs squad with Victor Wembanyama playing the way he is. However, before the blowout came, the Spurs would have to get through a sluggish first half borne of both poor shooting from both teams and a heavy whistle. After hitting 3-5 from three before the first timeout, including both of Wemby’s attempts for an 11-3 lead, both teams were sluggish, with the Spurs up shooting 33% in the quarter and the Blazers just 25%. But Portland got hot to close the quarter while the Spurs got sloppy, closing on a 7-0 run to cut the lead to two, 22-20. After barely playing last night, Carter Bryant brought a spark to the start the second quarter with a couple of corner threes and a block of Damian Lillard. Meanwhile, the Blazers did a good job of drawing fouls and were in the bonus less than four minutes in. It didn’t take long for the Spurs to join them, and what was already a sluggish game came to a screeching halt with all the whistles and free throws. Overall, the teams combined for 41 free throws in the half, and at one point, the Spurs scored 11 straight points from the stripe before a Stephon Castle alley-oop and consecutive Junliam Chamapgnie threes in the final minutes got the offense going again, and they went into the half up 64-49. The lack of whistles allowed the offenses to open up in the second half, but the Spurs were red hot, especially Wemby, who finished the night with 29 points on 9-13 shooting (3-6 from three) in just 24 minutes of play. An 11-0 run capped off by a technical foul on Deni Avdija gave the Spurs their first 20-point lead of the game, and there was no stopping them from there. The Blazers had nothing left in the tank, and the crowd watched in stunned silence as the Spurs got the lead all the way up to 30 for the first time this season on a Dylan Harper banker late in the third quarter. The last 15+ minutes of the game was entirely garbage time, and the Spurs finished their most dominant game of the season with a 125-103 win. Game Notes We finally got a glimpse of last season’s version of Luke Kornet. He was active in his first stint with a floater, two rebounds and block of a Chris Youngblood three-point shot, and the Spurs added a point to the lead. Granted, most of his time was spent against Yang Hansen, but he needed a confidence-booster, and maybe this was it. He finished the night with 6 points and 4 rebounds in 15 minutes, and perhaps most notably, was a +9 while on the floor. As frustrating as all the whistles were for both sides in the first half, it was comical at times (granted it’s easier to laugh when your team is ahead). Some of the calls were mindbogglingly soft, and Wemby former Spurs teammate Sidy Cissoko got into a bit of a French Flop Fest, with both exaggerating contact to get whistles. To borrow a hilarious text from Jesus Gomez last night, “Sidy flopped three times, and Wemby said, ‘Hold my cabernet sauvignon’”. (He also shook the refs’ hands after the game, which I’ve never seen before, adding to the hilarity.) Random thought of the night while sitting through a blowout: David Jones Garcia is still with the team instead of joining his fellow two-way players in Austin to start the season, which seems odd, but perhaps the Spurs intend to make him their 15th player once enough time has passed that they can sign him without going over the luxury tax, so he’s staying with the main team? He really has nothing left to prove at the G League level, and he reportedly turned down more lucrative offers from overseas, so maybe there’s an agreement in place? Just my two cents. Play of the Game It wasn’t the prettiest play of the game, but when trying to get out of the slugfest and free-throw-a-thon that was the second quarter, sometimes it just takes plays like this. (You also know it’s your night when stuff like this goes in.) HOW DID STEPH SAVE THAT ⁉️ 📺 @DAZN pic.twitter.com/IdGiNW9lfA — San Antonio Spurs (@spurs) November 8, 2026 Up next: Monday 11/9 at Phoenix Suns 8:00 PM CT on DAZN

teamStories.detailText: PORTLAND, Ore -- — Victor Wembanyama scored 29 points and led the San Antonio Spurs to a 125-103 blowout win over the Portland Trail Blazers on Saturday night. Devin Vassell added 15 points for the Spurs (8-2) along with 14 each from Stephon Castle and Julian Champagnie , and 13 from Dylan Harper . Deni Avdija led the Blazers (6-3) with 15 points. Scoot Henderson added 13 points, along with 12 from Damian Lillard and 11 from Jrue Holiday off the bench. Yang Hansen had his first career double-double with 12 points and 10 rebounds. Wembanyama’s 29 points came in just 24 minutes, and he took just 13 shots, going 9 of 13 from the field and 3 of 6 from 3-point range. Up next Spurs: At Phoenix on Monday. The star edge rusher returned from a knee procedure and showed the difference he can make, racking up 3.0 sacks in the Rams’ 20-13 victory over the Commanders on Sunday afternoon. Garrett’s first sack also forced a fumble, as he poked the ball out from quarterback Jayden Daniels in the second quarter. That led to a field goal late in the half, which cut Washington’s lead to 10-6 at halftime. Garrett then had two more in the fourth quarter, one of which came after he’d just been flagged for an offside penalty. While Garrett starred on defense, receiver Puka Nacua paced the offense with 14 catches for 150 yards with a touchdown. His 14 receptions are the third-most he’s had in a single game in his career. Blake Corum ran it in for a 1-yard score to cap an eight-play, 69-yard drive. Stafford finished 26-of-43 for 228 yards with a TD and a pick. At 5-4, the Rams are now above .500 for the first time this season and on a three-game winning streak. The team will be on the road to face division-rival Arizona next weekend before a Week 11 bye. The Commanders have fallen to 2-5-1. They won’t have much time to think about their missed opportunities, as they’ll face the Giants on Thursday night in Week 10.

stories.title: Instant reaction: Broncos rally in fourth quarter to defeat Panthers in another nailbiter
stories.summary: The Denver Broncos were able to rally in the fourth quarter to defeat the Carolina Panthers 26-21. Here are some instant reactions from Denver’s big win.
stories.detailText: Nov 8, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Denver Broncos running back Jonah Coleman (20) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the second half at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Denver Broncos battled the Carolina Panthers this afternoon in their Week 9 matchup. It was a back-and-forth game between the two teams that came down to the final of quarter of play to find a winner. In the end, the Broncos came out on top registering another comeback victory to move to 7-2 on the season. Here are some instant reactions from today’s game. Broncos’ offense ignites in fourth quarter to seal the deal For the entire first half of the season struggling on offense, the Broncos had an opportunity to shine against the Panthers. Carolina entered today’s matchup sporting a bottom 5 run defense, a bad third down defense, and the second-worst red zone defense in the NFL. After scoring 10 first quarter points against the Panthers, things looked up for Denver’s offense. They dominated first half time of possession and notched 15 first downs and 159 yards of total offense. Unfortunately, a Bo Nix interception in enemy territory proved to be a big momentum change in the game. In addition to that, Denver’s interior offensive line was manhandled in the first two quarters. Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg struggled with Lee Hunter and Derrick Brown and Denver gained just 34 yards on the ground in the first half. The Broncos’ offense wasn’t on the field much in the third quarter. But as usual, four quarter heroics once again came into focus. Denver was able to carve out two scoring drives. The first was a 17-play drive that went 80 yards and was capped off with a Jonah Coleman touchdown run. On their next possession, Nix was able to hit Pat Bryant on a beautiful 26-yard touchdown throw. The touchdowns were great, but it was awesome to see Nix and the offense perform well on third down. They had a lot of big drive-sustaining conversions that made the final touchdowns possible. But that pitch to Coleman late in the game that could have cost Denver the win? Oof. That certainly raised the collective blood pressure of Broncos Country. I was hoping for more effectiveness in the ground game, but I’m happy to see Denver’s offense come together in the fourth quarter and ignite to lead the Broncos to victory. Their success was a big part of why they were able to get their fifth-straight victory of the season. Well done, offense! Beat up Broncos’ defense struggles, but does enough to hold off Panthers’ offense The Broncos entered today’s matchup with several key starters out on defense. The starting safety tandem of Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga were out, making Devon Key and J.L. Skinner the next men up. Defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike was also inactive after being placed on injured reserve. To make things worse, Riley Moss exited the game in the second quarter after suffering a concussion. Down four starters, Bryce Young and the Panthers’ offense was able to gain some steam and have success. Carolina reeled off back-to-back touchdown drives at the end of the first half and the start of the second half to take a 14 to 13 lead in the third quarter. Whether it was the pass or the run, Vance Joseph’s defense couldn’t find a way to get them off the field. Young had an impressive streak of fifteen-straight completed passes. A big issue all game long was the absence of a formidable pass rush which was quite a bit of a surprise. The Panthers entered today’s matchup allowing 23 sacks. Denver wasn’t able to take down Young until halfway through the four quarter when Jonathon Cooper came up big on third down and finally brought the fourth-year signal caller down. The defense had two big plays that saved their poor play throughout the contest. The first was when Key was able to intercept a pass in the endzone that bounced off Tommy Tremble’s right arm. To end the game, Nik Bonitto was able to strip sack Young in the final minutes of play to seal the deal for the Broncos. I’ll say this though, Denver giving up so many third-and-long plays, even with the injuries, was extremely concerning. I thought Joseph’s conservative playcalling late in the game was perplexing. The defense will have a lot of reflection to do over the bye week to rectify some of the issues we have seen recently, but I’m happy they were able to close the game out with a big turnover. Broncos enter bye week with momentum and a 7-2 record It’s incredibly hard to get a read on who this year’s Broncos are. However, they just keep finding ways to win. Today’s victory over the Panthers is their fifth in a row. They still maintain the AFC West lead with their victory today and hold their place as the second seed in the AFC’s tough playoff race. All things considered, the bye week couldn’t have come at a better time. It’s time for Denver to recalibrate, regroup, and find a way to fix their issues in the second half of the season.

stories.title: Panthers vs Broncos: Recap and reaction
stories.summary: The Carolina Panthers battled, but some bad penalties and bad luck resulted in a loss to the Denver Broncos, 26-20.
stories.detailText: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 08: Devon Key #26 of the Denver Broncos intercepts a pass during the third quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers battled, but some bad penalties and bad luck resulted in a loss to the Denver Broncos, 26-20. First Quarter The Broncos got the ball first and immediately marched it down the field. They ran the kickoff out past the 40 then took two deep shots. Neither connected, but the second drew a rather ticky tack pass interference call. Jonah Coleman broke off a few nice runs to quickly put the Broncos in goal to go. The defense stepped up there. They stopped a first down run then got pressure on Bo Nix on second and third down to force incompletions and a fourth down field goal. The Panthers offense did nothing outside of a first play completion to Mitchell Evans. The Broncos moved the ball quickly once again. A couple of chunk plays got them into Panthers territory. Lee Hunter had a couple of nice plays, but another pass interference extended the drive. A few plays later, Bo Nix hit Courtland Sutton on a quick slant for a touchdown. The Panthers went three and out after a near miss to Tetairoa McMillan and a bad route by Darren Waller. After the punt, Marco Wilson got called for a taunting penalty for standing over Jaylen Waddle after an incomplete pass. The quarter ended after Bobby Brown led a group of Panthers in the backfield for a tackle for loss. Second Quarter The defense got off the field on third and long to get the ball back. The offense finally moved into Denver territory with a completion to McMillan and a couple of good runs by Chuba Hubbard, the second of which drew a late hit at the end. The drive fell apart after that. Young was nearly picked by Riley Moss, then three players jumped early for a false start. They ultimately settled for a 43 yard field goal, which Ryan Fitzgerald pretty much shanked out to the right. The Broncos moved the ball into Panthers territory, aided by a pass interference by Marco Wilson, his fourth penalty of the game. He was bailed out this time though. A couple plays later, Corey Thornton skied to undercut a receiver for an interception. The momentum shifted a little bit from that point. Bryce Young picked up a 3rd and 15 with a deep comeback to McMillan. He found Darren Waller a few times over the middle to continue the march into Broncos territory. The offense was faced with a 4th and 1, and Chuba Hubbard broke free off the left side for a big game. A few plays later, Young found Tommy Tremble in the backfield corner of the end zone for a toe tapping touchdown. Ryan Fitzgerald actually made the extra point this time, but he followed that by kicking the ensuing kickoff out of bounds. That gave the Broncos a short field to manage a quick two minute drill into field goal range to make it 13-7 heading into the half. Third Quarter The Panthers got the ball first out of the half and carried their momentum from the end of the first half. Young found Waller out of the gate for a big gain. A nine yard run from Hubbard and a nine yard catch by Evans put the Panthers on the edge of the red zone. After a couple of ineffective plays, Young found Waller deep over the middle for a touchdown to put the Panthers up 14-13. The defense kept the good vibes rolling. They stuffed a couple of early down runs to force the Broncos into an obvious passing situation. They got quick pressure, which forced Nix to step up into the waiting arms of Pat Jones. Young continued to pick apart the Broncos defense with more help from Darren Waller. He also had a 15 yard scramble to help the drive along. The Panthers got inside the five. Young tried to find Tremble in the end zone, but the ball was batted away. It somehow landed on Tremble’s arm on the way to the ground and was caught by a Broncos defender for the unlikeliest of interceptions. And it probably should have been a defensive pass interference as well. Fourth Quarter The Panthers committed a couple of penalties to help the Broncos start their drive, and they were followed by a series of easy short to intermediate completions from Bo Nix. It was a 14 play drive and was capped off by Jonah Coleman running to the outside and stiff arming Corey Thornton to the ground on his way to a go ahead touchdown. The offense couldn’t muster a response. A run went nowhere, a pass was incomplete, then Monroe Freeling was blown by for a rapid sack to end the drive with haste. The defense looked like they got off the field after a few plays, but Corey Thornton was called for a pass interference on third down, and it was another pretty soft call. A few plays later, Nix found Pat Bryant completely uncovered for an easy 26 yard touchdown. Bryce Young led a march down the field. He connected with Chuba Hubbard on a fourth down slant for a clutch conversion to keep the drive alive. Things got bogged down from there, and the Panthers ended up in a 4th and 15 spot. Young found space, stepped up, and hit John Metchie down the field to pick up the first down. Young was hit in the head in the process, which added a few extra yards to put the Panthers inside the ten. On the next play, Young found McMillan open on a slant for a touchdown to make it a one score game. The defense needed a quick stop. They stopped Jonah Coleman on first down. On second, Coleman dropped a pitch and the ball went bouncing back towards the goal line. Coleman eventually fell on it, but it was a loss of 18 yards. The Panthers made the tackle on third and long and forced the Broncos to punt coming out of the two minute warning. Young hit McMillan on a slant for a 21 yard gain on the first play of the drive to move into the Broncos side of the field. There was an offsides Bronco, and penalty would have stopped the clock even if it was declined. Instead, the Panthers had to hurry to the line, and on the next play, Young was hit in the arm trying to throw the ball. He fumbled, and the Broncos recovered. They were able to pick up a first down to run out the clock. Overview The Panthers actually outplayed the Broncos on a play to play basis. They averaged 5.7 to the Broncos 4.8 yards per play. Penalties and mistakes were the difference. In the defense of the Panthers, some of the drive extending pass interference calls were very questionable. Also, the interception probably could have been a pass interference on Denver, and it was a complete fluke that the ball ended up in the hands of a Bronco. It’s a disappointing loss, but it was an admirable performance for such a banged up Panthers team against a 6-2 Broncos team. The Broncos are just a charmed team right now, and the Panthers couldn’t overcome whatever black magic voodoo Sean Payton has done to earn his team some good fortune. The Panthers travel to New Orleans to take on the Saints in a key divisional matchup.

stories.title: Broncos WR Jaylen Waddle, CB Riley Moss suffer concussions against Panthers
stories.summary: Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and cornerback Riley Moss both suffered concussions against the Panthers.
stories.detailText: CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and cornerback Riley Moss sustained concussions within minutes of each other in Denver's 26-21 victory over the Carolina Panthers on Sunday. The Broncos went into the game without either of their starting safeties as Brandon Jones (hamstring) and Talanoa Hufanga (ankle) were both game-day inactives. Second-year cornerback Jahdae Barron played in Moss' spot. Moss was injured as he made a tackle on Trevor Etienne in the second quarter. Waddle, who had one catch Sunday for 22 yards, left the game with seconds to go in the first quarter. He reached to make a catch in front of Panthers cornerback Marco Wilson and was hit by Zakee Wheatley , who knocked the ball free. Waddle, who has battled ankle and chest injuries already this season, jumped up after the play and walked toward the Broncos huddle but then left the field and did not return. He has 30 receptions for 337 yards and two touchdowns this season. The Broncos (6-2) entered the day with a slim lead in the AFC West race over the Kansas City Chiefs (5-2).

stories.title: Kenneth Walker scores 3 TDs as the Chiefs roll past the woeful Jets 35-12 to end their 2-game skid

stories.detailText: KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- — Patrick Mahomes threw for 242 yards with a pair of touchdown passes to Kenneth Walker, who added 102 yards and a score on the ground, and the Kansas City Chiefs got back on track with a 35-12 rout of the hapless New York Jets on Sunday. Walker finished with 143 yards from scrimmage and the Chiefs sacked Geno Smith five times while keeping the Jets out of the end zone, allowing Kansas City (6-2) to erase the stink of consecutive losses to the Seahawks and Broncos. Smith finished with 165 yards passing for the Jets (2-7), who lost their fourth straight. They were credited with minus-9 yards of offense in the third quarter, when Kansas City scored a pair of touchdowns that turned a 14-12 halftime lead into a comfortable victory. The Chiefs have beaten New York in each of their last three meetings. The Jets, missing star wide receiver Garrett Wilson to a concussion , were reduced to running the ball with Braelon Allen or Breece Hall — back from a quadriceps injury for the first time in five games — or having Smith throw short passes to rookie Omar Cooper Jr . They were able to move the ball that way for a while. They just couldn't get into the end zone. One week after Jason Sanders kicked four field goals in a loss to the Raiders, he made four in the first half alone in Kansas City. It would have been five had Sanders not missed from 53 yards with less than a minute to go in the first half. The Chiefs, meanwhile, lost a fumble when backup quarterback Justin Fields was trying a sneak on third-and-1. They lost another one when Mahomes was sacked by the Jets' David Bailey for the second time in three plays, leaving the two-time MVP flexing his throwing elbow in pain. And then they watched embattled kicker Harrison Butker miss yet another field goal in the first half. Butker actually missed twice: He got a do-over after missing from 56 yards because of a penalty, then missed again. It was thanks to Walker, who was largely held in check by Seattle and Denver, that Kansas City took a lead into the break. His first touchdown reception came on the first play of the second quarter, and his second was a 25-yard screen pass in which offensive guards Trey Smith and Kingsley Suamataia laid down a trail of pancakes for him to follow. Walker did most of the work on a 60-yard TD drive to start the second half, too, though it was a lateral by Mahomes along the line of scrimmage to Travis Kelce on fourth-and-goal at the New York 1 that finally got the Chiefs into the end zone. Kansas City put the game out of reach later in the third quarter, after a 69-yard punt return was wiped out by penalty. Walker carried six times on an eight-play, 82-yard march, and his touchdown run made it 28-12 and gave him his third career three-TD game. Injuries Jets: Wilson (concussion) was inactive. So were LB Trevin Wallace (groin), DE Joseph Ossai (ankle) and CB Nahshon Wright (back). Chiefs: CB Mansoor Delane (shoulder) and DL Peter Woods (concussion) were inactive. RT Jaylen Moore hurt his ankle. WR Xavier Worthy left in the closing minutes with a left hamstring injury. Up next Jets: Face Buffalo at home next Sunday. Chiefs: Visit Atlanta next Sunday. ------ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

stories.title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders loss to Rams in NFL Week 9
stories.summary: Here’s what we learned about the Commanders after a Week 9 clash with the L.A. Rams after watching it live
stories.detailText: The Commanders entered Week 9 officially in now-or-never mode. Washington had but two wins entering Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams. They were still in the mix despite an unreal rash of injuries to star players, due to a poor-playing NFC East. They needed to start stacking wins, especially with a massive upcoming clash with the New York Giants next Thursday night. That meant beating the super-talented (and also injury-plagued) Rams. Washington was not able to do that. The Commanders had a shot to win at the end but came up just short in a 20-13 loss to the Rams at Northwest Stadium. Let’s examine some key takeaways from Sunday’s clash with the Rams after watching it live: Winning time doesn’t work Washington entered Sunday’s fourth quarter all tied up with the Rams. That game status didn’t last long. Puka Nakua – the receiver was a Commanders killer – made a leaping touchdown catch to give Los Angeles its largest lead of the day, however slim it may have been. It was a big moment for the Commanders to respond. They weren’t able to do that, coming up short on third down and then passed on a 58-yard field goal attempt for a punt. The long ensuing Rams started working the clock against Washington as the clock dipped below six minutes. The Commanders didn’t have momentum on their side. They scored 10 points in the first two drives and just three points over the next seven. That was not, well, great. Jayden Daniels was able to work the ball into Rams territory, but then Myles Garrett struck. The Rams edge rusher — he had three sacks — flashed past rookie center Matt Gulbin for a huge sack and a 12-yard loss. Euro-step for the sack is crazy 😭 📺 @NFLonFOX | #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/3jkz7Jbriv — Los Angeles Rams (@RamsNFL) November 8, 2026 Daniels’ fourth-down pass was a deep that was a short and allowed former Washington first-round pick Emmanuel Forbes to knock it away. Washington forced a three-and-out and got the ball back with roughly a minute left. Antonio Williams’ fair catch inside the 10-yard line left a long way to go. The distance was cut in half with a 41-yard gain Stefon Diggs. Washington couldn’t get much farther and ended failing on that final drive. D efense continues creating turnovers Say what you want about the Commanders defense and its’ frustrating inconsistency, but coordinator Daronte Jones’ offense has been good taking the ball away. The were ranked 10 with 1.4 turnovers created per game. They did better than that on Sunday against the Rams. The first one came at the end of the first half, when K’Lavon Chaisson punched the ball out and Nick Cross recovered it. stories.title: Rams-Commanders final score: Did Myles Garrett help the Rams win in Week 9?
stories.summary: The Rams won their third game in a row, and Myles Garrett earned three sacks
stories.detailText: The Los Angeles Rams beat the Washington Commanders by a final score of 20-13 in Week 9 of the NFL season. Chris Shula finally had Myles Garrett back, and Garrett returned to the Rams brilliantly with a forced fumble to go along with three sacks, including a massive sack in the fourth quarter to nearly put away the game. Euro-step for the sack is crazy 😭 📺 @NFLonFOX | #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/3jkz7Jbriv — Los Angeles Rams (@RamsNFL) November 8, 2026 Garrett looked terrific in his return, and it was needed while the Rams offense continued to struggle to dominate as well as their overall defense did. There’s been a theme of Shula’s defense keeping the Rams in games until Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford get going on offense, and that trend continued in Week 9. The overall offensive play in this game started slow with each team exchanging field goals early to knot the game at 3-3. The Rams started especially stagnant as they failed to convert a third down in the first two quarters. Washington scored the only first half touchdown when Jayden Daniels found former Ram Van Jefferson to take a 10-3 lead over L.A. Jefferson had a solid day against his former team with his TD score and some big grabs. Jefferson ended up with more receiving yards than anyone on the Rams outside of Puka Nacua. The Rams wouldn’t find the endzone until the second half as their offense struggled mightily for any positive consistency outside of Nacua and some credit to Blake Corum for looking like the best running back for the Rams today. Corum scored for the fifth game in a row in Week 9 when he scored L.A.’s first touchdown after halftime. Later on, Stafford would find Nacua to help the Rams take a 20-13 lead. The Commanders gave L.A. a scare on their final drive of the day as Stefon Diggs got loose for a long grab with under a minute to go, but the Rams defense survived, and the team escaped with a win. As it a pretty for L.A.? Not at all, but they did enough to keep their playoffs hopes alive as the NFL season heads towards Week 10. The Rams are 5-4 and will look to get to 6-4 in their next matchup against the Arizona Cardinals. The Cardinals beat the Rams earlier in the year, but in Week 9 the Rams won, and they’ll go from there.
